items.q: Which best captures the relationship between data and information?
options: Information is processed/organised data; information depends on data, not vice-versa
Information is always smaller than data
items.explain: Data = raw unorganised facts; information = data processed/organised/given context. Information depends on data; data does not depend on information.

items.q: A DBMS is a general-purpose software system that facilitates which four processes?
options: Defining, constructing, manipulating, and sharing databases
items.explain: A DBMS facilitates DEFINING (types/structures/constraints → metadata), CONSTRUCTING (storing data), MANIPULATING (query/update/report), and SHARING (concurrent multi-user access).

items.q: The real-world domain that a database models is called the:
items.explain: A database is a logically coherent collection of related data representing some aspect of the real world — the mini-world or Universe of Discourse (UoD).

items.q: In a banking transfer, the requirement that debit and credit must BOTH happen or NEITHER does addresses which file-system problem?
items.explain: Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing: a failure after debiting A but before crediting B leaves an inconsistent state. The DBMS guarantees atomic transactions with automatic rollback.

items.q: Storing a double-major student's details once per department in a file system causes:
items.explain: Duplicating data across files wastes space and risks inconsistency when one copy is updated. A DBMS uses a central store to minimise redundancy.

items.q: Two modes of database use are OLTP and OLAP. OLTP is characterized by:
options: Complex analytical queries for business decisions
Many users performing small, frequent retrievals/updates
items.explain: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) = many users, small retrievals/updates (banking, airlines). OLAP = analytical processing for decisions/predictive models, using data mining.

items.q: Ensuring 'every enrolment refers to a valid student' is which kind of data integrity?
items.explain: Referential integrity = a reference must point to something that exists. Entity = unique ID; domain = valid value range; user-defined = business rules.

items.q: The three levels of data abstraction, from lowest to highest, are:
items.explain: Physical (how data is stored) → Logical/conceptual (what data + relationships) → View/external (part relevant to a user). Lowest = physical, highest = view.

items.q: Modifying the storage/indexes WITHOUT changing the logical schema is enabled by:
items.explain: Physical data independence = change the physical schema without altering the logical/conceptual schema. Logical data independence (harder) = change logical schema without affecting applications.

items.q: The difference between schema and instance is best described as:
options: Schema is the data; instance is the design
Schema is the design (changes rarely); instance/state is the data at a moment (changes frequently)
items.explain: Schema = overall design (like variable declarations). Instance/state = the actual data at a particular moment (like variable values). Many states correspond to one schema.

items.q: The three-schema architecture's three levels are:
items.explain: ANSI three-schema = External (user views) / Conceptual (logical structure) / Internal (physical storage). The mappings between them provide data independence.

items.q: The four phases of database design, in order, are:
items.explain: Requirements specification → Conceptual (ER model) → Logical (relational + normalization) → Physical (indexes, storage). Abstract to concrete.

items.q: A key security advantage of three-tier over two-tier client-server architecture is:
options: Clients cannot directly access the database server (only via the middle tier)
It removes the need for a database
items.explain: In three-tier, the application/web server holds business logic and clients reach the DB only through it — the DB server is not directly accessible, enhancing security.

items.q: A user who books a movie ticket through a predefined interface without DB knowledge is a:
items.explain: Naïve (parametric) users interact through canned interfaces without knowing the DB internals. Sophisticated users write their own SQL; the DBA manages the database.

items.q: Which architecture stores data across multiple physical locations for scalability and fault tolerance?
items.explain: Distributed databases spread data across multiple locations/nodes, providing scalability, fault tolerance (replication), and performance. Centralized = one server.

items.q: In an ER diagram, a multivalued attribute is represented by a:
items.explain: Multivalued attribute = double ellipse; derived = dashed ellipse; key = underlined; relationship = diamond.

items.q: Age computed from Date_of_Birth is an example of a ___ attribute, shown as a ___:
items.explain: Age is DERIVED from the stored attribute DoB, so it is not stored. A derived attribute is drawn as a dashed ellipse.

items.q: The 'grade' a student earns in a course is best modelled as:
options: A descriptive attribute of the 'enrolls' relationship
items.explain: Grade exists only when a student enrolls in a course, so it is a descriptive attribute of the 'enrolls' relationship (on the diamond), not of either entity.

items.q: An attribute that can be subdivided into smaller parts (e.g. address → street, city, state) is:
items.explain: A composite attribute can be split into sub-parts (address, name). A simple/atomic attribute cannot be subdivided.

items.q: A relationship in which the SAME entity set participates more than once (e.g. course prerequisites) is:
items.explain: A recursive relationship relates an entity set to itself (course→course prereq, employee→supervisor). Role names label the lines to disambiguate.

items.q: The number of entity sets participating in a relationship set is its:
items.explain: Degree = number of participating entity sets. Binary = degree 2 (most common); ternary = degree 3.

items.q: Total participation of an entity in a relationship is shown in an ER diagram by:
items.explain: Total participation (every entity must participate) is shown by a double line. Partial participation uses a single line.

items.q: In (min, max) notation, a line from Student to Enrolls labelled (2, 5) means a student can enroll in:
options: At most 2 and at least 5 courses
A minimum of 2 and a maximum of 5 courses
items.explain: (min, max) = (2, 5) means minimum 2, maximum 5. min=1 would imply total participation; max=N implies no upper limit.

items.q: A minimal superkey is called a:
items.explain: A candidate key is a minimal superkey (no attribute removable). The DBA chooses one candidate key as the primary key.

items.q: For a many-to-many binary relationship set, the primary key is:
options: The union of both entities' primary keys
items.explain: M:N → union of both PKs. 1:1 → either entity's PK; 1:N/N:1 → the 'many' side's PK. (Descriptive attributes like grade are not part of the PK.)

items.q: A weak entity set is uniquely identified by:
options: The owner's primary key + its own discriminator (partial key)
items.explain: A weak entity has no PK of its own; its PK = identifying (owner) entity's PK + a discriminator. It has total participation in a many-to-one identifying relationship.

items.q: In an ER diagram, a weak entity set and its identifying relationship are drawn as:
items.explain: Weak entity = double rectangle; identifying relationship = double diamond; discriminator = dashed underline.

items.q: When mapping a 1:N relationship to a relational schema, you:
options: Put the PK of the 'one' side as a foreign key in the 'many' side's relation
Merge both entities into one table
Store a set in one column
items.explain: 1:N → foreign key on the MANY side (the 'one' side's PK becomes an FK in the 'many' table). No new table needed.

items.q: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship is mapped to:
options: A foreign key on one side
A new junction relation containing both entities' primary keys
items.explain: M:N → a brand-new junction table with both PKs (composite PK) + any relationship attributes. A single FK can't capture M:N.

items.q: A multivalued attribute is mapped to a relational schema by:
options: Storing a comma-separated list in one column
Creating a separate relation holding the attribute plus the entity's PK
items.explain: A multivalued attribute becomes its own table (attribute + entity PK), because a relation can't hold a set in one cell (1NF). e.g. instructor_phone(ID, phone).

items.q: The relational algebra SELECT operator (σ):
items.explain: σ (select) filters ROWS by a predicate (a horizontal partition). ∏ (project) chooses COLUMNS. Note: SQL's keyword SELECT actually does projection.

items.q: The PROJECT operator (∏) in relational algebra always:
options: Removes duplicate tuples (since relations are sets)
items.explain: ∏ keeps the listed columns and removes duplicate tuples, because a relation is a set. ∏rating(Sailors) returns each distinct rating once.

items.q: Relational algebra is said to be 'closed' because:
options: Every operation produces a relation, which can be input to further operations
It only works on closed sets
items.explain: Closure: each operation takes relations and produces a relation, so operations compose into expressions. It is a procedural language.

items.q: Two relations are union-compatible if they have:
options: The same arity AND compatible attribute domains
items.explain: Union-compatible = same number of attributes (arity) and the i-th attributes have compatible domains. Required for UNION, INTERSECTION, DIFFERENCE.

items.q: Which set operation is NOT commutative?
items.explain: Set difference: R − S ≠ S − R in general. Union and intersection are both commutative and associative.

items.q: The relational algebra operator used to express 'find sailors who reserved EVERY boat' is:
items.explain: Division answers 'for all / every' queries: (∏sid,bid Reserves) ÷ (∏bid Boats) gives sailors paired with every boat. Keyword 'all/every' → division.

items.q: A Cartesian product R × S of relations with n and m attributes produces a relation with:
items.explain: Cartesian product: degree = n + m, size = |R| × |S| (every tuple of R paired with every tuple of S). Usually meaningless until filtered by a selection.

items.q: A natural join (⋈) is equivalent to:
options: A Cartesian product followed by a selection on common columns (with the duplicate column removed)
items.explain: Natural join = Cartesian product internally + automatic match on common-named compatible columns + drop the duplicate column — removing the cross-product's redundancy.

items.q: To compute 'average age per rating' you use grouping with the grouping attribute placed:
options: To the left of ℱ, with aggregates to the right
items.explain: In ℱ notation, the grouping attribute is on the LEFT and aggregate functions on the right: rating ℱ AVG(age)(Sailors). This is SQL's GROUP BY.

items.q: SQL's four sub-languages are DDL, DML, DCL and TCL. INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE belong to:
items.explain: DML (Data Manipulation Language) = INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE. DDL = CREATE/ALTER/DROP; DCL = GRANT/REVOKE; TCL = COMMIT/ROLLBACK.

items.q: The difference between CHAR(10) and VARCHAR(10) is:
options: CHAR is variable-length, VARCHAR is fixed-length
CHAR is fixed-length (pads with spaces); VARCHAR is variable-length (no padding)
items.explain: CHAR(n) is fixed-length — 'Avi' in CHAR(10) is stored as 'Avi' + 7 spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable-length — stores just 'Avi'.

items.q: BLOB and CLOB are large-object types. The difference is:
options: BLOB stores binary data (images/video); CLOB stores large character data (text)
BLOB stores text; CLOB stores binary
items.explain: BLOB = Binary Large Object (images, audio, video); CLOB = Character Large Object (large text/documents). The DATE format in SQL is YYYY-MM-DD.

items.q: What is the key difference between DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE TABLE?
options: DROP removes data AND the table structure; TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure
TRUNCATE removes the structure; DROP keeps it
DROP can be filtered with WHERE
items.explain: DROP deletes data + structure (constraints/indexes gone); TRUNCATE empties all rows but keeps the table structure (and resets AUTO_INCREMENT). Both are DDL.

items.q: Which command changes the STRUCTURE of an existing table (e.g. add a column)?
items.explain: ALTER TABLE modifies structure (ADD/MODIFY/DROP/RENAME columns, add/drop constraints). UPDATE changes data values, not structure.

items.q: The rule that a primary key value cannot be NULL is the:
items.explain: Entity integrity = PK cannot be NULL. Key constraint = PK cannot be duplicated. Referential integrity = FK must match an existing PK (or be NULL).

items.q: A FOREIGN KEY declared 'ON DELETE CASCADE' means that deleting a parent row:
options: Sets the child foreign keys to NULL
Sets the child rows to their default value
items.explain: CASCADE propagates the delete to child rows. Other actions: NO ACTION (reject, the default), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT.

items.q: A PRIMARY KEY constraint is equivalent to:
items.explain: PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, and only one per table. UNIQUE alone marks a candidate key and allows one NULL.

items.q: In an SQL query, the WHERE clause corresponds to which relational algebra operation?
items.explain: WHERE = Select (σ, row filter); the SELECT clause = Project (∏, columns); FROM = the relation(s)/joins. SQL's SELECT keyword does projection, not selection.

items.q: Executing 'DELETE FROM employee;' (with no WHERE clause) will:
options: Delete all rows in the table
items.explain: DELETE without WHERE removes ALL rows (but keeps the structure — unlike DROP). Always scope DELETE/UPDATE with WHERE unless you mean 'all'.

items.q: When mapping an M:N relationship that has its own attribute (e.g. advisor with Date_of_assignment) to relations, where does that attribute go?
options: Into the new junction (bridge) table, alongside the two foreign keys
In a separate table of its own
items.explain: A relationship attribute describes the pairing, not either entity, so it becomes a column of the junction table whose composite PK is the two entities' PKs (e.g. Advisor(Instructor_ID, Student_ID, Date_of_assignment)).

items.q: Which is the correct way to add a named foreign key to an already-existing column in MySQL?
options: ALTER TABLE student ADD FOREIGN KEY
ALTER TABLE student ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES department(dept_id)
items.explain: ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT name FOREIGN KEY (col) REFERENCES parent(col) adds a named FK to an existing table; the referencing column must already exist. Naming it allows dropping it later and is needed for multi-column FKs.
